verdicts.label: Declaration
verdicts.msgid: Override 1: the policies. ODRL 2.2 lets each policy declare a conflict strategy with {code0}: {code1} (permissions override prohibitions), {code2} (prohibitions override permissions) or {code3} (the policy is void if any conflict is detected). These terms were checked against the ODRL 2.2 vocabulary and the pinned JSON-LD context (folio-assistant-core {code4}). When every applicable policy declares the same strategy, the table uses it. A policy that declares none counts as {code5}, the owner's default D. If the applicable policies declare different strategies, {code6} is {code7}. ODRL 2.2 says a policy with several conflict values (after a merge or inheritance) is void when its rules conflict (W3C ODRL Information Model 2.2, Policy Conflict Strategy). This IG treats the applicable policies of one request as merged. The only declaration that changes an outcome is {code8} declared by every applicable policy. ODRL's own default when nothing is declared is {code9}, but the outcome is the same: with a conflict, {code10} voids the policy and {code11} denies, and both are refused.
verdicts.reason: an agreement's declaration in the guide's policy merge is not the harness's Declaration node.

verdicts.label: Reference
verdicts.msgid: The fourth layer (L4: Executable—reference applications and services) focuses on software applications and services within a digital ecosystem. It is intended to include executable reference software that accurately represents the intentions, operational, and functional requirements of the WHO recommendations; addresses user and health system needs; and comprises machine-readable data and calculations within interoperability standards, as documented in the L1–L3 layers. As a fully functional application, it is intended to serve as a generic starting point, ready to be localised to the specific operational context of the users, population, and health system within which it is deployed. Additional products at this layer include terminology services to support consistent data representation for interoperability; reusable software libraries including software development kits; application programming interfaces; and function as a service to support updates to FHIR content and capabilities across subscribed digital systems.
